title: אבא בר אבא הכהן אבוה דשמואל

paragraphs: Abba bar Abba the priest, father of Shmuel. (1) He was called “Shmuel’s father” because of an incident reported in Halakhot Gedolot, Laws of Divorce: Shmuel’s father went to the West. A woman [מדיתא; designation unresolved] who knew the language of birds encountered him. She said, “Have intercourse with me, and I will give you such-and-such a sum,” because she knew that a great man would issue from him. He fled from her and came, by means of the Name, that night to his wife, had intercourse with her, and went away again. Eventually it became known that she was pregnant. They brought her to court and flogged her. Shmuel, in his mother’s womb, said, “I will bend my head, lest the tip of the whip reach my head and hurt me.” He bent his head in his mother’s womb, and the tip of the whip reached him. End quotation. Something of this appears in Tosafot, Kiddushin 73a. (The book Gilgulei Neshamot (G.N.), letter pe, writes: “This woman [מדיתא in Heilprin’s report] was a reincarnation of Potiphar’s wife, who solicited Joseph because she knew that a great man would issue from intercourse with him.” End quotation.) Gilgulei Neshamot (G.N.), letter alef, writes: “Shmuel’s father: why was he called after his son? The explanation is that Shmuel’s father is Samuel of Ramah, and his son Shmuel is a reincarnation of Saul. Just as Saul spoke with Samuel after Samuel’s death, so Shmuel’s father spoke with his son Shmuel (see there) after his own death, as in Berakhot 18b. Just as the woman, the medium, said, ‘Whom shall I bring up for you?’, so they said to him, ‘There are many Abbas here.’ Just as Samuel told Saul, ‘Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me,’ so Shmuel’s father told his son Shmuel, ‘You will soon come to us.’ Just as he said to Saul, ‘With me—in my company,’ so Shmuel’s father said, ‘I laughed because you are highly esteemed in this world.’ Shmuel is a reincarnation and spark of King Saul. Thus Shmuel was called ‘Arioch, a king,’ for the law follows Shmuel in civil matters.” End quotation. (A numerical hint: the letters of אריוך מלך, with the number of the letters and two inclusive units, total the numerical value of שאול.) My lord father wrote in his work: “Samuel of Ramah was from the feminine side; therefore Hannah said, ‘Give Your maidservant male offspring’: she made him dependent on his mother (Megalleh Amukkot, ofan 140). Since Abba, Shmuel’s father, is Samuel of Ramah, they called him ‘Shmuel’s father’: that is, he [Shmuel] depends on his father, rather than his mother, because he is not from the feminine side.” End quotation; the words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious. (That is: unlike Abba, who is Samuel of Ramah and was from the feminine side, this Shmuel depends on his father; hence Abba was called Shmuel’s father.) My lord father wrote: “For this mystery Hannah said, ‘I have lent him’: the holy spirit flashed within her, for her son Samuel was Saul’s father.” See Yalkut on Samuel, section 80.

(2) He was a pious man, keeping orphans’ property in the middle of his own money (Berakhot, chapter Mi Shemeto; 18b; see below, Shmuel). Shabbat 65a: he would not allow his daughters, etc. Bava Metzia 24b: he found donkeys in the wilderness and returned them to their owners after twelve months, beyond the strict requirement of the law. Avodah Zarah 20b: the Angel of Death told him, “Were I not concerned for the dignity of people, I would lay bare the place of slaughter.”

(3) In Shocher Tov on Samuel, chapter 10, and Yalkut there, remez 100: Abba traded in silk. Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira sent to him from Nisibis that he wished to buy silk. He held the silk for Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira. Later the latter did not wish to take it, saying, “I sent you mere words.” Abba said, “Your words are more trustworthy to me than money; therefore I relied on you and did not wish to sell to another.” Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira blessed him to merit a son like Samuel of Ramah, of whom it is written, “All Israel knew that Samuel was trustworthy.” Thus Abba merited this son, Shmuel bar Abba. End quotation. Zayit Ra'anan writes: “Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira lived while the Temple stood, as is evident from the incident of the Kuti who ate Passover offerings in Jerusalem; Shmuel was in the third generation after the destruction. Perhaps he lived so very long.” End quotation. See what I wrote under Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira. It appears that this Abba lived long, for Abba sent a question to Rabbi Yehudah Nesia, etc., and Rabbi Yehudah Nesia sent back, etc., out of respect for him, so as not to establish Shmuel’s father as mistaken (chapter Ha'ishah Shalom, 115, end of b). Rabbi Yehudah Nesia permitted the oil of the Kutim; Rav would not eat it, and Shmuel told him, “Eat; otherwise I will write against you as a rebellious elder,” as in the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter Ein Ma'amidin (see below, Rabbi Yehudah Nesia). Rabbi Yehudah Nesia was Rabbi’s grandson, and Shmuel was Rabbi’s physician (see there). Shmuel died shortly after his father’s death, as appears from Berakhot: they called Shmuel one who consumed orphans’ money; presumably this was immediately after his father Abba’s death. Shmuel went to the courtyard of death (see the account at length below, Shmuel), and his father wept there because he would die soon.

(4) Shmuel’s father asked Shmuel, who answered him, etc.; his father then said to him, “If so, you were mistaken” (Zevachim 26a). He sent to Rabbi, “Let our master teach us,” and Rabbi replied, “Thus said Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yose in his father’s name” (Pesachim 103a). Rav raised an objection to Shmuel’s father, who fell silent; Rav applied to him, “Princes restrained their words and placed a hand over their mouths” (Ketubbot, chapter 4, 51b). It appears that Rav’s raising an objection to Shmuel’s father indicates that Rav was his student. This also seems so because Rav was Shmuel’s colleague and Shmuel received teaching from his father, as I wrote there. But Me'ilah 9a requires examination: Shmuel’s father and Rabbi Avin raised an objection to Rav Huna. Rav Huna was Rav’s student: how could he object to Rav Huna, his student’s student? One cannot say that this was Rav Huna the exilarch, who died in Rabbi’s days, for it says that Shmuel’s father and Rabbi Avin asked Rav Huna, and Rabbi Avin was not in Rabbi’s time (see there). Later new Talmud editions were printed: “and Ravin” was deleted; another reading does not read “to Rav Huna.” This pleased me (see above, the introduction). In the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter Hacholetz, halakhah 11, Abba bar Vava disagrees with his son Shmuel; the same subject appears in Niddah, first chapter, halakhah 4, as Abba bar Abba disagreeing with his son Shmuel. Thus know that the Jerusalem Talmud often calls Abba “Vava.” In its chapter Tamid Nishchat, halakhah 2, Rabbi Yochanan says, “On this Abba bar Abba told me.” In Shekalim, chapter 2, halakhah 5, the reading is “On this Abba b.A. entered,” meaning that he objected. Shmuel’s father and Levi entered the synagogue of Shaf Veyativ in Nehardea and prayed there (Rosh Hashanah 24b; Avodah Zarah 43b). (Benjamin’s Book of Travels writes that in the city Shefita is a synagogue built of stones and earth from Jerusalem.) He delivered a funeral oration over Levi; see there. Rosh Hashanah 27b–28a: they sent to Shmuel’s father. Shabbat 108b [source: ר״ח, 208b; corrected from the matching passage]: Mar Ukva and Rabbi Mattanah spoke in his name. His daughters [Shmuel’s, in the cited account] were captured, etc.; they entered before Rabbi Chanina. This one said, “I was captured but am pure,” etc.; he told Rabbi Shemen bar Abba the priest, “Attend to your relatives.” See Mari bar Rachel, Shmuel’s daughter. Pinchas was his son; this requires examination.
